cards.meaning: Having a strong effect or power, especially a medicine, drink, force, or combination of things.
cards.nuance: It can describe anything that produces a powerful effect. In medicine, it may simply mean strong, while in other contexts it can suggest unusual strength or influence.

uses.sentence: The agency offered a potent mix of bold ideas and careful research.
uses.tip: Often describes a striking or unusually effective combination.

uses.where: Dinner conversation · trying a new drink
uses.sentence: That coffee was potent; I was wide awake after one cup.
uses.tip: Common for strong drinks, medicines, or spices with a powerful effect.

uses.sentence: Her examples were potent because they turned an abstract issue into something memorable.
uses.tip: Pairs naturally with images, examples, arguments, forces and combinations.

origin.summary: From Latin potens, meaning powerful or able, related to potere, meaning to be able or have power.

timeline.text: Potens means powerful or able and develops from potere, to have power or be able.
Potent appears in English in senses connected with power and strength.
It describes powerful medicines, drinks, forces, combinations and persuasive examples.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse potent with potential: a potent effect is already powerful, while potential means the possibility of becoming powerful.

cards.register: Formal, but also used in everyday speech
cards.meaning: Exceptionally large in amount, impressive in scale, or showing remarkable ability.
cards.nuance: The word suggests something stands far above what is ordinary. It can describe enormous quantities, rapid progress, or a person with exceptional talent, but it often carries a note of admiration.

uses.sentence: The team made prodigious progress after simplifying the approval process.
uses.tip: Use it for progress or results that are far more impressive than expected.

uses.sentence: Their youngest child has a prodigious memory for song lyrics.
uses.tip: It can warmly praise an exceptional talent, though it may sound slightly old-fashioned.

uses.sentence: Revenue showed a prodigious increase following the launch of the new service.
uses.tip: It fits formal reports and essays when you want to emphasise dramatic scale.

origin.summary: From Latin prodigiosus, meaning ‘marvellous’ or ‘monstrous’, based on prodigium, a sign or portent that seems impossible.

timeline.text: Prodigious develops from prodigium, meaning ‘a portent or extraordinary event’, and prodigiosus, meaning ‘marvellous’.
The word enters English with senses connected with wonders, extraordinary size and monstrous qualities.
It mainly describes exceptional scale, achievement or ability.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it merely for anything large; it suggests a scale or achievement that is unusually impressive.

cards.meaning: Present in a large or excessive amount.
cards.nuance: It can sound complimentary when describing generous quantities, but critical when the amount is unnecessary or out of control.

uses.sentence: The research team offered profuse praise, but gave us very little evidence for the proposed changes.
uses.tip: Often criticises praise or apologies that seem excessive rather than sincere.

uses.sentence: There were profuse apologies for the delayed speeches, but the evening was warm and generous.
uses.tip: Natural for praise, apologies, flowers or other things produced in abundance.

uses.sentence: The ceremony was marked by profuse displays of gratitude and affection.
uses.tip: Sounds polished in essays and reports; use abundant or plentiful for a less formal tone.

origin.summary: From Latin profusus, meaning ‘poured forth freely’, which developed from profundere, ‘to pour out’.

timeline.text: Profusus originally described something poured out freely or in large quantities.
The word enters English in senses connected with abundance and excess.
It means existing in large or excessive amounts.

cards.pitfall: Profuse is often mildly critical: a profuse amount of praise may sound exaggerated, while abundant can be more neutral.

cards.meaning: The degree to which something is near or close to another person, place, or event in space or time.
cards.nuance: It often emphasizes how close something is, especially when distance affects convenience, safety, or relationships. It can sound more formal than “closeness,” particularly in workplace or technical contexts.

uses.where: Office planning · choosing a meeting room
uses.sentence: The proximity of the meeting room to the main office made it a convenient choice.
uses.tip: Use it when the exact distance is less important than how close or convenient something is.

uses.sentence: She enjoys the proximity of the park, the shops, and the train station.
uses.tip: A slightly formal alternative to “how close” or “nearby.”

uses.sentence: The property’s proximity to public transport is one of its main advantages.
uses.tip: Common in property, planning, and business writing when describing access to nearby places.

origin.summary: From Latin proximitas, meaning nearness, which was based on proximus, the nearest or closest.

timeline.text: Proximitas develops from proximus, meaning nearest or closest.
The word enters Middle English in the sense of nearness.
It describes closeness in space, time, or relationship and is common in formal contexts.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse it with “approximate,” which means close to an exact value but not exact. “In close proximity to” is also redundant in many contexts.

cards.meaning: So small, weak, or insignificant that it has little effect or value.
cards.nuance: The word often expresses impatient dismissal, although it can simply describe something physically or numerically small. It sounds harsher than “small” and more judgemental than “minor.”

uses.sentence: The team had a puny budget and no realistic chance of finishing the project on time.
uses.tip: Use it when a limited amount of money, time, or support is clearly inadequate.

uses.sentence: That was a puny portion for someone who had just run five miles.
uses.tip: It sounds informal and slightly teasing, so keep it among people you know well.

uses.sentence: A puny increase in sales did little to offset the falling subscription numbers.
uses.tip: Use it in analysis when the result is not only small but too weak to matter much.

origin.summary: From French puny, meaning small or insignificant, which was connected to Latin puniceus, a term associated with Carthage.

timeline.text: Latin puniceus referred to Carthage or the Carthaginians.
French develops puny in the sense of small, inferior, or insignificant.
The word enters English and becomes established as a general adjective.

cards.pitfall: Do not use “puny” merely to say that something is physically small; it suggests that the size makes it weak, inadequate, or unworthy of attention.

cards.register: Common in formal and descriptive writing
cards.meaning: Spreading or occurring in a way that is uncontrolled and difficult to stop.
cards.nuance: Usually critical: it suggests that a problem has grown far beyond reasonable limits. It can also describe vigorous growth or activity, but that use is less common.

uses.sentence: Rampant scope creep left the team with three priorities and no clear deadline.
uses.tip: Use it to describe a negative trend that has become seriously uncontrolled.

uses.sentence: Rumours were rampant after my sister changed her job without telling anyone.
uses.tip: A natural choice for gossip, rumours or other problems spreading quickly.

uses.sentence: The article examines the rampant spread of misinformation during an election.
uses.tip: Often appears before a noun such as spread, growth or misinformation.

origin.summary: From Old French rampant, originally describing a creature rearing up on its hind legs and later developing the sense of being violent or unchecked.

timeline.text: The Old French word appears, including in heraldic descriptions of animals rearing up on their hind legs.
English adopts it for wild, violent or aggressive behaviour.
It broadens to describe anything growing or spreading without restraint.

cards.pitfall: It normally has a negative tone, so don’t use it for healthy growth or enthusiastic activity without clear context.

cards.meaning: A particular area of activity, knowledge, experience, or authority.
cards.nuance: Often suggests a distinct world or field that someone enters or works in. It can sound formal, especially in phrases such as “beyond the realm of possibility.”

uses.where: Team briefing · entering a new market
uses.sentence: The company is entering the realm of sustainable packaging with this new product line.
uses.tip: Use it when you are describing a new area of business or expertise.

uses.where: Dinner conversation · trying a new hobby
uses.sentence: I never thought I’d venture into the realm of baking, but my sourdough starter is thriving.
uses.tip: A slightly playful way to describe an unfamiliar activity or social world.

uses.sentence: Changing the payment terms falls outside the realm of my authority, so please contact the finance director.
uses.tip: Pair it with “of” to identify the field or limit being discussed.

origin.summary: Realm comes through Old French from Latin regnum, meaning “kingdom” or “rule.” Its original sense was a kingdom, but it later developed the broader meaning of an area or domain.

timeline.text: Regnum means “kingdom,” “rule,” or “dominion.”
The word reaume enters French with the sense “kingdom.”
Realm first appears in English with the meaning “kingdom.”
It is also widely used for an area of activity, knowledge, or authority.

cards.pitfall: A realm is not limited to physical territory; it usually means a field, experience, or area of authority.

cards.meaning: To fill something again or restore supplies that have been used up.
cards.nuance: Often used for stock, shelves, accounts, or energy levels. It suggests making something available again rather than replacing it completely.

uses.sentence: Please replenish the coffee and paper before the afternoon shift arrives.
uses.tip: Common when stock, materials, or shared supplies need topping up.

uses.where: At a gathering · preparing for guests
uses.sentence: We need to replenish the snacks before more people arrive.
uses.tip: Natural for food, drinks, and other items that have been consumed.

uses.sentence: The team replenished its reserves after a busy quarter.
uses.tip: Use the past form for an event and the present form for an ongoing need.

origin.summary: From Latin replenescere, meaning ‘to fill again’, built from re-, ‘again’, and plere, ‘to fill’.

timeline.text: Replenescere forms from re-, ‘again’, and plere, ‘to fill’.
The word enters English and is used for filling supplies or restoring what has been used.
It is common in practical contexts involving stock, funds, reserves, and supplies.

cards.pitfall: Replenish means to fill or restock what is already there; it does not usually mean to replace an entire object.

cards.meaning: Full of something, especially a quality, feature or supply of something.
cards.nuance: This sounds polished and slightly literary rather than everyday. It is often used with “with” and can suggest that something is richly filled or richly detailed.

uses.sentence: Her proposal was replete with practical examples, so the client immediately saw the value.
uses.tip: Use it when you want to emphasise that a proposal, report or plan contains many useful elements.

uses.sentence: The dining tables were replete with flowers, candles and carefully chosen seasonal food.
uses.tip: It adds an elegant, descriptive tone to a scene that is full of abundance.

uses.sentence: The report is replete with evidence that the new training programme improved productivity.
uses.tip: A useful alternative to “full of” when you want a more formal, polished style.

origin.summary: From the Latin repletus, meaning “filled,” which came from replere, “to fill.” The word entered English in the 1600s.

timeline.text: Repletus meant “filled” and was based on replere, “to fill.”
The word began appearing in English, initially in formal and literary writing.
It is mainly used in formal contexts, especially in the pattern “replete with.”

cards.pitfall: Do not confuse it with “replicate,” which means to reproduce something or occur more than once.

cards.register: Common in formal writing; slightly formal in speech
cards.meaning: Present in large numbers or found in great abundance, often to the point of being excessive.
cards.nuance: Usually has a negative tone, especially when describing problems, rumours or mistakes. It can also mean widely common, but the sense of “full of” is much more familiar.

uses.sentence: Rumours about the layoffs were rife after the announcement, so the team asked for clear guidance.
uses.tip: Use it for rumours, problems or mistakes that seem to be happening everywhere.

uses.where: Dinner conversation · exaggerating a busy week
uses.sentence: Traffic was rife across the city, so our journey took twice as long as expected.
uses.tip: In conversation, “rife with” often sounds more natural when describing something filled with problems.

uses.sentence: The report notes that misinformation was rife online before the correct figures were published.
uses.tip: It adds a formal, slightly forceful tone to statements about widespread problems.

origin.summary: The word probably comes from Old Norse and originally meant “to tear”; its modern sense developed through the idea of something being torn or spreading everywhere.

timeline.text: Its ancestor was connected with the sense “to tear” or “break apart”.
The word appeared in English with meanings connected with tearing and being widespread.
It settled into its familiar sense of being common or present in abundance.
It is especially common in the phrase “rife with” and often describes problems or rumours.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse “rife” with “ripe”: “rife” means common or abundant, while “ripe” usually means ready to eat or fully developed.

cards.register: Common in formal and technical writing
cards.meaning: To fill something completely with liquid or make it hold as much as it can.
cards.nuance: It can also mean to overwhelm people, a market or a message with too much of something. The figurative use often suggests excess.

uses.sentence: We can’t saturate every channel with launch messages and still expect people to notice them.
uses.tip: Use the figurative sense when the amount of communication becomes excessive.

uses.where: After heavy rain · planning a picnic
uses.sentence: The lawn is saturated after all that rain, so we should skip the picnic.
uses.tip: Here it means completely soaked and unable to absorb much more water.

uses.sentence: Avoid saturating the proposal with every possible metric and lead with the three that matter.
uses.tip: It sounds blunt, so use it when you want to criticise an overloaded document.

origin.summary: From Latin saturare, meaning ‘to fill to capacity’, connected with satur, meaning ‘sated’ or ‘filled’. English borrowed the word in the 1500s.

timeline.text: saturare means ‘to fill to capacity or make sated’.
The word enters English with meanings involving filling something or making someone sated.
It is used for soaking, filling to capacity and overwhelming with too much.

cards.pitfall: In business, saturated often means that a market has little room for growth; it does not simply mean very busy.

cards.register: Common in writing and formal speech
cards.meaning: Existing as one thing rather than several, or so unusual that it stands out.
cards.nuance: It can mean a single, individual focus, especially for something that should be shared or divided. In formal contexts, it can also mean remarkable or exceptional.

uses.sentence: The project needs a singular goal, not five competing priorities.
uses.tip: Use this when concentrating attention on one clear objective.

uses.sentence: She has a singular talent for making strangers feel welcome.
uses.tip: This polished use means exceptionally noticeable or impressive.

uses.sentence: The novel presents a singular vision of life in a small coastal town.
uses.tip: Pair it with vision, style, focus or purpose for an elevated tone.

origin.summary: From Latin singulus, meaning single or individual, through Old French singulier.

timeline.text: The root singulus meant one apiece, single or individual.
The word enters English through French in the sense of single or individual.
It develops the related sense of exceptional, unusual or standing apart.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use singular merely to mean one; in everyday speech, a single item may sound more natural.

cards.register: Common in formal and professional English
cards.meaning: A large number of similar things happening or arriving over a short period of time.
cards.nuance: It often suggests an overwhelming amount, especially of complaints, requests, changes or other events. The phrase “a spate of” is the usual pattern.

uses.sentence: We’ve had a spate of requests for dark mode, so it’s worth adding to the next development cycle.
uses.tip: Use it when several similar items arrive faster than the team can manage them.

uses.sentence: After the announcement, there was a spate of messages asking everyone for their availability.
uses.tip: It sounds slightly formal, but it can add emphasis to a busy or crowded moment.

uses.where: Email to colleagues · reporting recent incidents
uses.sentence: The office has experienced a spate of minor break-ins, although no valuable items were taken.
uses.tip: It works well in reports and news writing to show a sudden cluster of events.

origin.summary: The word probably began as a word for a sudden flow or flood of water and later developed its modern sense of a large number of similar things.

timeline.text: It first appeared in English with meanings connected with a torrent or rushing flow.
The sense broadened to include a sudden large amount of anything arriving together.
It is mainly used in the pattern “a spate of” for complaints, incidents, requests or similar events.

cards.pitfall: Usually use it with “a” and “of,” as in “a spate of complaints,” rather than saying someone “did a spate.”

cards.meaning: Extremely rich, expensive, and luxurious in appearance or quality.
cards.nuance: Often describes food, rooms, clothing, or celebrations that look exceptionally lavish. It can sound admiring, but sometimes suggests extravagance.

uses.sentence: The client loved the sumptuous dining room, although it felt slightly too formal for our team.
uses.tip: Use it for impressive settings, but consider whether the tone suits the occasion.

uses.sentence: We were welcomed into a sumptuous hall filled with flowers, candlelight, and gold-trimmed chairs.
uses.tip: It paints a vivid picture of luxury and works especially well with food, décor, and furnishings.

uses.sentence: Our suite was sumptuous, with velvet curtains, a marble bathroom, and a panoramic view of the river.
uses.tip: Pair it with rich materials, elaborate food, or spacious surroundings to make the description vivid.

origin.summary: From Latin sumptuosus, meaning expensive or luxurious, based on sumptus, meaning expense or expenditure.

timeline.text: Sumptuosus describes something costly, extravagant, or luxurious.
The word enters English with meanings connected with expense and luxury.
It chiefly describes something richly luxurious or visually impressive.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it for anything merely comfortable or attractive; it suggests exceptional luxury.

cards.meaning: Unnecessary, especially because there is already more than enough.
cards.nuance: It can sound precise and mildly critical, so use it when extra detail or resources add little value.

uses.sentence: The final chart is superfluous because the key figures are already highlighted in the table.
uses.tip: Use it for something that can be removed without losing value.

uses.sentence: Would you mind if we left the extra wine at home? It would be superfluous with all that food.
uses.tip: It is more natural in prepared or formal speech than casual conversation.

uses.sentence: We removed the third appendix because its technical detail was superfluous for this audience.
uses.tip: Useful in professional writing when you want to justify cutting unnecessary material.

origin.summary: From Latin superfluus, meaning ‘overflowing’ or ‘excessive’, formed from super- ‘over’ and fluere ‘to flow’.

timeline.text: Superfluus develops from super- ‘over’ and fluere ‘to flow’.
The word enters English with meanings connected with excess or overflow.
It is used for anything unnecessary because there is already enough.

cards.pitfall: It is more formal than ‘not needed’ and can sound critical, so avoid using it about people’s choices without tact.

cards.meaning: A sudden, sharp increase or movement in amount, activity, emotion, or price.
cards.nuance: A surge is stronger and faster than a normal rise, often with a feeling of urgency or intensity. As a verb, it describes a sudden increase or upward movement.

uses.sentence: We saw a surge in online orders after the product appeared in a short video.
uses.tip: Use it for a sudden rise that is noticeable or difficult to handle.

uses.sentence: A surge of excitement passed through the room when the host announced the surprise party.
uses.tip: A surge of emotion is a common and vivid expression.

uses.sentence: The website experienced a surge in traffic on Monday, followed by a gradual decline.
uses.tip: It suits reports that need to emphasize a brief, sharp rise.

origin.summary: The word comes from Latin surgere, meaning ‘to rise’, and entered Middle English through Old French.

timeline.text: Latin surgere, ‘to rise’, provides the root for the word.
Middle English borrows surge from Old French, referring to an upward movement or swelling.
The meaning broadens to include sudden increases in quantity, activity, emotion, or price.
Surge commonly describes a rapid, noticeable rise or upward movement.

cards.pitfall: A surge is more sudden and forceful than a simple increase, so it may not suit a gradual rise.

cards.meaning: Of little importance, difficulty or significance.
cards.nuance: It can describe a small practical matter, but often suggests that something is too easy to deserve serious attention.

uses.sentence: The formatting issue is trivial compared with the deadline we’re facing.
uses.tip: Use it to put a problem into perspective without making it sound too insignificant.

uses.sentence: It seemed trivial at first, but the delay affected everyone.
uses.tip: Useful when you’re reconsidering something that initially looked unimportant.

uses.sentence: I’ve left out the trivial details so we can focus on the main decision.
uses.tip: Common in formal writing when explaining what has been omitted or prioritised.

origin.summary: From Latin trivialis, meaning ‘commonplace’, originally related to the trivium, the meeting place of three roads and later the simplest part of medieval logic.

timeline.text: Trivialis develops from trivium, meaning ‘crossroads’ or ‘meeting place of three ways’.
The trivium becomes the simplest branch of the seven liberal arts, associated with ordinary or elementary learning.
The word enters English and gradually shifts toward meaning ‘of little importance’.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it for anything you simply dislike; it focuses on importance or difficulty, not personal preference.

cards.meaning: Continuing at full strength without weakening or slowing down.
cards.nuance: It suggests that an activity, pressure or feeling remains intense. Use it when the force or pace has not diminished despite time, effort or obstacles.

uses.sentence: Customer interest remained unabated even after the launch was delayed by two weeks.
uses.tip: Use it to describe sustained demand, pressure or effort.

uses.where: Football match · talking about the final minutes
uses.sentence: The home side’s enthusiasm was unabated, and they kept singing until everyone had left.
uses.tip: It can describe strong feelings that continue without fading.

uses.sentence: The storm continued unabated overnight, leaving several roads closed across the region.
uses.tip: Common in formal reporting about storms, conflict, pressure or activity.

origin.summary: Formed in English from the prefix un-, meaning ‘not’, and abate, meaning ‘to lessen or bring down’.

timeline.text: Abate appears in English with the sense of ‘to lower, weaken or bring down’.
Unabated begins to be used for something that is not reduced in force.
It commonly describes continuing intensity, pressure or activity.

cards.pitfall: Unabated describes something that continues at full strength; it does not simply mean ‘unchanged’.

cards.register: Common at work and in writing
cards.meaning: Applying to everyone or every part of a particular group or situation.
cards.nuance: It suggests broad relevance or applicability. It can also mean something works in all countries, cultures or contexts.

uses.sentence: The new wellbeing allowance is available to all employees on a universal basis.
uses.tip: Use it to show that a rule or offer applies across an entire workforce.

uses.sentence: Music has a universal appeal, even when the words and instruments change from place to place.
uses.tip: Common before words such as appeal, truth, concern and experience.

uses.sentence: The survey found that access to clean water remains a universal concern across every region studied.
uses.tip: Use it for an issue or principle that is relevant everywhere, not just locally.

origin.summary: From Latin universalis, meaning ‘of or concerning the whole universe’, formed from universus, ‘all or the whole’.

timeline.text: Universalis develops from universus, meaning ‘the whole’ or ‘all collectively’.
The word enters Middle English in scholarly and legal writing.
It is used for things that apply to everyone, everywhere or across an entire group.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse universal with unanimous: unanimous means everyone agrees, while universal means something applies to everyone.

cards.meaning: Completely without anything that makes a bad situation less serious or easier to bear.
cards.nuance: This is a strong, formal word used for disasters, failures and problems that receive no relief at all. It can sound blunt or exaggerated, so it is best reserved for genuinely severe situations.

uses.sentence: The system outage was an unmitigated disaster for the support team.
uses.tip: Use it when there is no practical way to reduce the damage.

uses.sentence: Rain, lost luggage and a flat tyre made the journey an unmitigated nightmare.
uses.tip: It adds emphasis, but may sound more dramatic than the story warrants.

uses.sentence: The flood caused unmitigated damage to several small businesses in the town.
uses.tip: It fits formal reports when the harm was total and no relief was provided.

origin.summary: From Latin mitigare, ‘to make milder’, with the English prefix un- added to express the opposite.

timeline.text: Mitigare means ‘to make milder or less severe’.
The word mitigate enters English in the sense of reducing severity or hardship.
Unmitigated becomes established as a formal adjective meaning completely unrelieved.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it for ordinary inconveniences; it describes a situation with no relief at all.

cards.meaning: Too large, complicated, or awkward to handle easily.
cards.nuance: Often describes equipment, processes, or systems that are difficult to use or manage. It can also refer to topics or situations that feel hard to control.

uses.sentence: The approval process has become too unwieldy for small purchases.
uses.tip: Use it to describe a process that has become complicated and inefficient.

uses.sentence: We hired a van because the old sofa was too unwieldy to carry downstairs.
uses.tip: It is a natural choice for something physically awkward or difficult to move.

uses.sentence: The integration plan proved unwieldy, so we divided it into smaller stages.
uses.tip: In writing, it can sound more precise than simply ‘difficult’ or ‘complicated’.

origin.summary: Formed in the Middle English period from the un- prefix and wieldy, meaning easy to handle or control.

timeline.text: The root wieldan meant to control or handle; its related adjective developed the sense of manageable.
Unwieldy emerged with the sense of not being easy to handle, move, or manage.
It commonly describes objects, systems, or situations that are awkward to handle or control.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it simply to mean heavy or large; the key idea is that something is difficult to handle, move, or manage.

cards.meaning: Very large in physical size or in the amount of information, material or detail.
cards.nuance: It suggests considerable bulk or length and sounds more formal than words such as large or extensive.

uses.sentence: The proposal is voluminous, so we should focus on the sections that affect the budget.
uses.tip: Useful when describing a document, report or collection that contains a lot of material.

uses.sentence: The novel is voluminous, but its many subplots gradually come together.
uses.tip: Often describes books, archives or collections that have substantial size or length.

uses.sentence: The researcher draws on a voluminous body of evidence from several countries.
uses.tip: Pairs naturally with body of evidence, collection, archive and amount of material.

origin.summary: From Latin voluminosus, meaning bulky or full of rolls, which developed from volumen, a roll or large book.

timeline.text: Voluminosus is formed from volumen, meaning a roll or large book.
The word enters English with senses connected with bulk, rolls and large books.
It mainly describes great size or a large amount of content.

cards.pitfall: Voluminous usually suggests bulk or length rather than wordiness; use verbose for something written with too many words.
